verdict.winner: Standing seam metal leads on lifespan and freeze-thaw resistance, architectural asphalt shingles lead on value, and natural slate ranks highest for historic homes, per the InterNACHI chart and Josten Roofing.
verdict.reasoning: Standing seam metal ranks first for durability — its 40-80-year life and snow-shedding panels resist New Jersey's ~35-45 freeze-thaw cycles and ~110-115 mph design wind (ASCE 7-16), spreading its $9.00-$16.00 NJ per-square-foot cost across decades, per InterNACHI and Josten Roofing.
verdict.alternate: Architectural asphalt shingles rank first on value at $6.50-$11.00 per NJ square foot (Josten Roofing) with a 30-year life; TPO leads for flat roofs through heat-welded seams, and natural slate leads for historic homes at a 60-150-year life, per the InterNACHI chart.

keyFacts: Standing seam metal is a concealed-fastener steel or aluminum panel system that sheds snow and lasts 40-80 years, per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart.
Architectural asphalt shingles are a laminated fiberglass-mat covering that lasts 30 years and install at $6.50-$11.00 per square foot in NJ, per Josten Roofing and InterNACHI.
Natural slate is a quarried-stone covering with near-zero porosity that resists freeze-thaw across a 60-150-year life, at $10-$30 per square foot in NJ, per InterNACHI.
Standing seam metal installs at $9.00-$16.00 per square foot in NJ, per Josten Roofing.
Cedar shake lasts 20-40 years and cedar shingle 30-50 years (CSSB / Cedar Shake & Shingle Bureau); InterNACHI lists a 25-year general wood life.
Clay and concrete tile itself lasts 100+ years, but the underlayment limits the system's service life, per InterNACHI and the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance.
TPO membrane carries a 7-20-year InterNACHI life (15-25 in practice), with heat-welded seams and a reflective white surface, per InterNACHI.
EPDM rubber lasts 15-25 years, stays flexible in cold, and is puncture-resistant, per the InterNACHI chart.

Standing seam metal and natural slate both carry near-zero water absorption, so the roughly 35-45 freeze-thaw cycles each north-NJ winter (regional climate estimates) cannot crack them, per the InterNACHI chart.

Standing seam metal's 40-80-year life outlasts asphalt by decades; freeze-thaw stresses fasteners and long-run thermal expansion rather than splitting the covering, per InterNACHI and NRCA expansion guidance.
Natural slate failures trace to corroded fasteners or degraded valley flashing rather than the stone, across a 60-150-year life, per InterNACHI and the National Slate Association.

Architectural asphalt shingles lose protective granules over time across their 30-year life; lower-grade clay and concrete tile risk freeze-thaw spalling, per InterNACHI and the Tile Roofing Industry Alliance.
Standing seam metal and architectural asphalt shingles both exceed the ~110-115 mph design wind speed mapped for northern NJ under ASCE 7-16, per ASCE wind maps.

Standing seam metal sheds the ~31.5-inch average annual snowfall (NOAA 1991-2020 normals, ~78% falling December-February) off interlocking panels, though shed snow needs snow guards over Newark entryways, per NOAA normals.

Architectural asphalt shingles hold snow until melt and rely on an ice-and-water barrier at the eaves, required to extend at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line under IRC R905.1.2, to block ice-dam backup, per the IRC as enforced through N.J.A.C. 5:23.
A reflective roof stays over 50 degrees F cooler than a conventional roof on a sunny afternoon, per the U.S. Department of Energy.

A reflective metal finish lowers roof surface temperature through high solar reflectance and thermal emittance (not added R-value), cutting peak cooling demand 11-27% in air-conditioned buildings, per the EPA and the Cool Roof Rating Council; Newark's heating-dominated Climate Zone 4A carries a winter heating offset, per the DOE.
TPO reflects solar energy off its white surface and meets cool-roof reflectance-and-emittance levels measured per ASTM C1549 and listed by the CRRC, per the CRRC and DOE.
3-tab asphalt shingles last 20 years and trail on uplift resistance, per the InterNACHI chart.

Longest-lasting NJ roofing materials rank: natural slate 60-150 years, then clay or concrete tile 100+ years, then standing seam metal 40-80 years, then architectural asphalt 30 years and 3-tab 20 years, per the InterNACHI chart.
sources: InterNACHI (Standard Estimated Life Expectancy Chart for Homes)
ASCE 7-16 / ASCE wind maps (~110-115 mph design wind, northern NJ)
NOAA 1991-2020 climate normals (~31.5-inch average annual snowfall)
U.S. Department of Energy (reflective roof temperature; Climate Zone 4A)
njContext: The NJ Uniform Construction Code treats a full re-roof of any material on a detached 1- or 2-family Newark home as ordinary maintenance — no permit — per N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7.

IRC R905.1.2 (enforced through N.J.A.C. 5:23) requires the ice-and-water barrier to extend at least 24 inches inside the exterior wall line, protecting Newark eaves against ice-dam backup driven by the ~31.5-inch average snowfall and ~35-45 freeze-thaw cycles.
Northern NJ's ~110-115 mph design wind speed under ASCE 7-16 sets the uplift that standing seam metal and architectural asphalt exceed, per ASCE wind maps.
Standing seam metal snow-shedding requires snow guards over Newark entryways given the ~31.5-inch average annual snowfall, per NOAA normals.
Architectural asphalt shingles install at $6.50-$11.00 per square foot in NJ (Josten Roofing); standing seam metal $9.00-$16.00; natural slate $10-$30 per square foot.
A full NJ roof replacement runs $10,000-$25,000, per HomeAdvisor NJ.

Architectural asphalt shingles fit color-and-budget-driven Essex County homes; standing seam metal suits long-hold owners; natural slate at a 60-150-year life fits pre-1920 / 1930s-1940s Essex County homes.

For NJ commercial flat roofs, TPO ($8.00-$12.00 per NJ square foot, Josten Roofing) fits most buildings and EPDM is the cold-flexible budget alternative; standing seam metal fits sloped, long-hold commercial structures.
Commercial roof work exceeding 25% of roof area within 12 months triggers a permit under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7.
Newark sits in heating-dominated Climate Zone 4A, so a reflective roof's summer cooling benefit carries a winter heating offset, per the DOE.
